subject: English
source: National Curriculum Year 6 English and KS2 SATs content domains (reading 2a-2h, GPS test format); Drive English folder held no KS2 material so content is original

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Grammar, punctuation and vocabulary (SATs skills)
lessons.title: Word classes and the GPS paper
objectives: Name the main word classes and spot them in sentences
Understand the layout and question types of the KS2 GPS test

keywords.def: the group a word belongs to, such as noun, verb or adverb
a word that introduces a noun, such as the, a, my, some
a word such as because or although that joins a clause to a main clause
a word or phrase that adds information about a verb

starter: Say bismillah. Underline the verb: The children walked to the mosque.
Write a sentence with a relative clause.
Correct: We was happy and them books were lost.

teach.heading: Why GPS matters
bullets: Paper 1: grammar and punctuation, about 45 minutes
Skills help your reading and writing too
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and explain the plan for the half term. The SATs are taken in May; today we start the skills we need. Reassure pupils: the test measures what we have learnt, and regular practice will help. Show the question types: tick, circle, underline, rewrite, insert punctuation.

teach.heading: Eight word classes
teach.note: Run a quick-fire on mini-whiteboards. Give example words and ask for the class. Misconception: pupils think each word always has one class. Show 'run' as a verb ('I run') and a noun ('a morning run').

teach.heading: Clues to word class
bullets: Nouns follow the, a or my
Adverbs often tell how, when or where
teach.note: Teach tests: Can I put 'the' before it? Can I change its tense? Show the sentence 'The tall boy ran quickly across the field' and label each word.

teach.heading: Phrases and clauses
bullets: A phrase has no verb and subject
A clause has a subject and a verb
A main clause makes sense alone
teach.note: Give examples: 'in the garden' (phrase), 'the boy ran' (clause), 'because he was late' (subordinate clause). Explain subordinate clauses depend on a main clause.

teach.heading: Test strategies
bullets: Check how many answers you need
Check by reading the sentence aloud
teach.note: Practise a sample question: 'Circle the adverb in this sentence.' Teach how to work out marks from the number of answers needed.

practice: Label the word classes: The old man walked slowly home.
Is 'because he was late' a main clause or subordinate clause?
Circle the preposition: The cat slept under the table.
independent: Complete a ten-question word class quiz.
Underline the subordinate clause in six sentences.
Write two sentences using the word 'run' as a verb and a noun.
exit: Name the word class of 'quickly' in: She walked quickly.
What is a determiner? Give one.
lessons.homework: Write ten sentences using different word classes and label each one.
lessons.send: SEND: use colour coding for word classes. EAL: build a word class glossary with pictures. Stretch: find words that belong to more than one class and write sentences for each.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Grammar, punctuation and vocabulary (SATs skills)
lessons.title: Active and passive voice
objectives: Explain the difference between active and passive sentences
Convert sentences between active and passive

keywords.def: the subject does the action: The boy kicked the ball
the subject has the action done to it: The ball was kicked by the boy
who or what the sentence is about
the person or thing that does the action

starter: Bismillah. Name two word classes.
Label: The cheerful girl sang loudly.
Underline the subordinate clause: We stayed in because it rained.

teach.heading: Active sentences
teach.note: Introduce the active voice as the usual way of writing. Ask who does the action in 'The dog chased the cat'. Pupils identify subject, verb, object.

teach.heading: Passive sentences
bullets: The action is done to the subject
The cat was chased by the dog.
teach.note: Show how the object becomes the subject. Highlight 'was chased' as the passive verb. Explain that 'by the dog' is optional. Passive can be 'The cat was chased.'

teach.heading: The test
bullets: If yes, it is probably passive
teach.note: Teach this test. Warn about the misconception that passive means past tense: 'The window is broken' (present passive) and 'The boy broke the window' (active past). Ask pupils to classify further examples.

teach.heading: Why use the passive?
bullets: When the doer is unknown or unimportant
Used in formal writing and reports
teach.note: Show examples from reports and notices: 'Visitors are asked to remove their shoes.' Discuss why active is often clearer in stories. Link to formal tone.

teach.heading: Changing voice
bullets: Active to passive: swap subject and object
Passive to active: find the doer
Check the verb tense stays the same
teach.note: Model converting 'The chef cooked the meal' to 'The meal was cooked by the chef'. Pupils practise on whiteboards. In SATs, they might be asked to rewrite a sentence in the active voice.

practice: Active or passive: The letter was posted yesterday.
Rewrite as passive: The teacher marked the books.
Rewrite as active: The ball was kicked by Zayd.
independent: Sort twelve sentences into active and passive.
Convert eight sentences between voices.
Write a short notice for the school website using the passive.
exit: Rewrite in the active voice: The cake was eaten by the guests.
What is the 'by' test for passive?
lessons.homework: Find five passive sentences in a newspaper or book and rewrite them as active.
lessons.send: SEND: use colour for subject, verb and object. EAL: model the pattern with be + past participle. Stretch: explain how the passive changes emphasis.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Grammar, punctuation and vocabulary (SATs skills)
lessons.title: Formal and informal register; the subjunctive
objectives: Distinguish formal from informal language
Recognise and use the subjunctive form

keywords.def: the level of formality in language
careful language used in letters, reports and speeches
a verb form used for wishes, demands and unreal situations: If I were
a shortened word with an apostrophe, such as don't

starter: Bismillah. Active or passive: The door was opened.
Rewrite in the passive: The pupils cleaned the hall.
Write a sentence with a relative clause.

teach.heading: Formal and informal
bullets: Formal: Would you be so kind as to assist me?
Match the language to the reader
teach.note: Discuss when each is appropriate: talking to friends vs writing to the headteacher. Link to adab: speaking respectfully to elders and teachers. Note that informal is not rude, just different.

teach.heading: Features of formal writing
teach.note: Provide a casual message and edit it into a formal one. Replace 'get' with 'obtain', 'help' with 'assist', 'big' with 'considerable'.

teach.heading: The subjunctive: if I were
bullets: If I were you, I would apologise.
Use were, not was, for unreal situations
teach.note: Explain that the subjunctive is used for unreal or hypothetical situations. In SATs, pupils may be asked to choose the correct form. Misconception: 'If I was you' is common in speech but not formal Standard English.

teach.heading: The subjunctive: demands
bullets: The head insisted that every pupil wear a badge.
It is vital that she be on time.
The verb stays in its base form
teach.note: Show 'He suggested that she bring a pen'. The verb after 'that' is in its base form, not 'brings'. Pupils compare 'The teacher requires that he is quiet' with the subjunctive 'be quiet'.

teach.heading: Choose the register
teach.note: Read three short texts: a text message, a letter to a head, a news report. Identify the register of each. Rewrite one in a different register.

practice: Make this formal: Can I have another go?
Choose: If I (was/were) taller, I would play basketball.
Complete: The imam asked that everyone ___ (be/is) quiet.
independent: Rewrite six informal sentences in formal English.
Complete eight subjunctive sentences with the correct verb form.
Write a formal request to the headteacher about a school trip.
exit: Choose the correct form: If she (was/were) here, she would help.
Name two features of formal writing.
lessons.homework: Write a formal email to ask for information about a visit and then write the same in an informal style.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence frames for formal requests. EAL: build a bank of formal vocabulary. Stretch: write three sentences using the subjunctive with insist, suggest and demand.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Grammar, punctuation and vocabulary (SATs skills)
lessons.title: Colons and semi-colons
objectives: Use a colon to introduce a list or explanation
Use a semi-colon to join related main clauses and to separate list items

keywords.def: a punctuation mark (:) that introduces a list, explanation or example
a mark (;) that links two closely related main clauses
a clause that can stand alone
a series of items

starter: Bismillah. Make formal: Can you get me a pen?
Choose: It is important that he (is/be) on time.
Add commas: My brother who is seven loves Lego.

teach.heading: The colon
bullets: You will need: a pen, a ruler and a notebook.
The part before the colon must be a full clause
teach.note: Show correct and incorrect examples. 'We need: pens' is wrong in formal writing if the part before the colon is not a complete clause. Model 'We need three things: a pen, a ruler and a notebook.'

teach.heading: Colon for explanation
bullets: Hamza was late: the bus broke down.
The second part explains the first
teach.note: Contrast colon use for lists with colon for explanation. Ask pupils to complete sentences: 'It was freezing: ...'.

teach.heading: The semi-colon
bullets: Zaynab loves reading; her brother prefers football.
Both parts must work as sentences
teach.note: Explain that a semi-colon is stronger than a comma and weaker than a full stop. Common error: using a semi-colon before a subordinate clause. Test: could each side stand alone?

teach.heading: Semi-colons in lists
bullets: We visited Cairo, Egypt; Madinah, Saudi Arabia; and London, England.
teach.note: Show that semi-colons prevent confusion. Provide a list with commas inside items. Pupils punctuate with semi-colons. This may appear as a SATs question about the function of a punctuation mark.

teach.heading: Choosing the right mark
teach.note: Play a quick game: hold up cards (colon, semi-colon, comma, full stop). Pupils choose the best mark for a sentence on screen.

practice: Add a colon: Bring the following to school a coat, a hat and gloves.
Add a semi-colon: The sun was shining the children were playing.
Which sentence is correct: It rained; so we stayed in. / It rained; we stayed in.
independent: Punctuate ten sentences with colons or semi-colons.
Write four sentences using a colon and four using a semi-colon.
Rewrite a list of places with semi-colons.
exit: What does a colon introduce?
Write a sentence using a semi-colon.
lessons.homework: Find examples of colons and semi-colons in books and explain how each is used.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight the main clauses on each side. EAL: build a punctuation function chart. Stretch: write a paragraph that uses both marks correctly.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Grammar, punctuation and vocabulary (SATs skills)
lessons.title: Dashes, hyphens, brackets and bullet points
objectives: Use dashes, hyphens, brackets and bullet points accurately
Explain the function of each mark

keywords.def: a short line (-) that joins words or avoids confusion
a longer line used to separate extra information or to mark a break
marks ( ) placed around extra information
a list where each point begins with a symbol

starter: Bismillah. Add a colon or semi-colon: I like tea my sister prefers juice.
Punctuate the list: you will need a pen a ruler and a book.
Add commas: Our teacher Mr Ali is kind.

teach.heading: Hyphens
teach.note: Show the difference between 'a man eating shark' and 'a man-eating shark'. Explain that hyphens may join words before nouns to act as a single adjective. SATs may ask to add a hyphen to avoid ambiguity.

teach.heading: Dashes
bullets: Mark extra information - like this - in a sentence
The door opened - and there stood Mum!
teach.note: Compare with brackets and commas. Use a pair of dashes for parenthesis. A single dash can add an afterthought. Beware of overuse.

teach.heading: Brackets
teach.note: Show brackets for explanations: 'The library (open until six) is free.' and 'Hana (my cousin) won.' Check that the sentence works without the brackets.

teach.heading: Bullet points
bullets: Keep the same grammar for each point
teach.note: Model a list: 'Pupils should bring:' followed by three points. Show an inconsistent list and ask pupils to fix it. Point out that the style must match across all items.

teach.heading: Which mark?
teach.note: Quick-fire practice: show five sentences and ask which mark would be correct. Explain that pupils must also be able to name the function of marks in the test.

practice: Add hyphens: a twenty five year old teacher
Add dashes: My uncle a very kind man visited us.
Which sentence needs a hyphen: a little used car / a little-used car?
independent: Complete a ten-question punctuation quiz.
Rewrite a notice using bullet points correctly.
Write six sentences with parenthesis using brackets, dashes and commas.
exit: Add a hyphen to avoid confusion: a small business owner (owner is small)
What is the function of brackets?
lessons.homework: Write a list of instructions for a game using bullet points and a lead-in colon.
lessons.send: SEND: sort cards by punctuation function. EAL: practise with sentences and pictures. Stretch: explain why a hyphen changes the meaning of a sentence.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Reading skills for the SATs - The Lighthouse
lessons.title: Reading paper skills: structure and retrieval
objectives: Understand the structure of the KS2 reading test
Answer retrieval questions accurately

keywords.def: find and write down information from a text
read quickly to get the general idea
look for specific words or facts
the type of reading skill being tested, such as 2b retrieval

starter: Bismillah. Add a hyphen: a well known writer.
Add brackets: The shop open until six is busy.
What does a colon introduce?

teach.heading: The reading test
bullets: Mix of multiple choice, short and longer answers
Time yourself: about 20 minutes a text
teach.note: Explain the test format. Questions follow the order of the text. Reassure pupils that they do not need to answer every question in a perfect way; practise using time well. Show the content domains (2a to 2h) in simple terms: vocabulary, retrieval, summarising, inference, prediction, structure, language effect, comparison.

teach.heading: Read the text
bullets: Read the title and any introduction
teach.note: Read the text in the note aloud once. Text - The Lighthouse (para 1) Maryam pressed her nose against the cold glass. Below her, the sea heaved and roared like a wild animal trapped in a cage. It was the third night of the storm, and her father had not slept since it began. (para 2) 'Keep the lamp burning, Maryam,' he had said, buttoning his heavy coat. 'If a ship sees our light, she will know where the rocks are.' Then he had stepped out into the darkness to mend the broken rail on the gallery. (para 3) Now the clock chimed eleven. Maryam's hands trembled as she trimmed the wick, but she did not let the flame flicker. Far out on the water, a tiny yellow light bobbed up and down. 'A ship!' she whispered. She grabbed the signal lantern and swung it three times, just as her father had taught her. (para 4) The light on the water paused, turned slowly, and began to creep away from the jagged rocks. Maryam let out a long, shaky breath and smiled. Tell pupils to number paragraphs and underline key words as they read.

teach.heading: Retrieval questions (2b)
bullets: Use the key word in the question
Scan for it in the text
Copy exact words if asked to find and copy
teach.note: Model: 'What did the clock chime?' Find 'clock chimed eleven'. Explain that retrieval answers are in the text and need accuracy. Misconception: adding opinion.

teach.heading: Mark allocation
bullets: 2 marks: two facts or a fact with explanation
Look at the number of lines
teach.note: Link marks to answer length. For a 2-mark question, give two points. Underline the question command words: find, give, explain, why.

teach.heading: Check your answer
bullets: Is it from the correct paragraph?
teach.note: Pupils practise self-checking. Ask them to prove each answer with the paragraph number. Mention that spelling matters less in reading but clear handwriting matters.

practice: How many nights had the storm lasted?
What was Maryam's father going to mend?
Find and copy a word that tells you the rocks were sharp.
independent: Answer six retrieval questions on The Lighthouse.
Underline the evidence in the text for each answer.
Write two retrieval questions of your own for a partner.
exit: What did Maryam swing three times?
Which paragraph tells us the time?
lessons.homework: Practise reading a short text and answering three retrieval questions.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight key words in the questions. EAL: pre-teach gallery, wick, jagged. Stretch: write 2-mark retrieval questions for a partner.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Reading skills for the SATs - The Lighthouse
lessons.title: Inference and prediction
objectives: Make inferences using evidence from the text
Make a prediction supported by evidence

keywords.def: an idea worked out from clues in the text
words or phrases from the text that support an idea
a statement about what may happen next
a hint in the text

starter: Bismillah. Find and copy: the time Maryam's clock chimed.
Add dashes: Her father a brave man left.
Name two punctuation marks used for lists.

teach.heading: What is an inference?
bullets: The author does not say it directly
We use clues to work it out
I think... because the text says...
teach.note: Remind pupils of inference from earlier years. Model: 'Maryam's hands trembled' tells us she was nervous or frightened. Show how to link the feeling to a quotation.

teach.heading: Inference: feelings
bullets: Evidence: 'hands trembled', 'did not let the flame flicker'
teach.note: Reread paragraph 3. Ask pupils to find phrases showing she was scared but responsible. A 2-mark inference answer needs the idea and the evidence.

teach.heading: Inference: reasons
bullets: Why did the ship turn away?
Because it saw the light and understood the danger
teach.note: Use paragraph 4. Ask pupils to answer in a sentence: 'The ship turned because Maryam's signal showed where the rocks were.' Mark points: reason and evidence.

teach.heading: Prediction
bullets: Use clues to say what happens next
teach.note: Ask what will happen next. Accept ideas that fit: her father returns, the storm ends. Evidence: 'the third night', 'broken rail'. Explain that predictions must be supported.

teach.heading: Writing it up
teach.note: Provide a frame. Model one full answer. Pupils write their own. Ask partners to check that the answer includes a quotation and an explanation.

practice: What does 'did not let the flame flicker' suggest about Maryam?
Why did Maryam's father tell her to keep the lamp burning?
What do you think will happen next? Give evidence.
independent: Answer six inference and prediction questions with quotations.
Write a paragraph about what Maryam is like using three pieces of evidence.
Predict the next paragraph in the story.
exit: Write an inference about Maryam's father using evidence.
What clue helps you predict what happens next?
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph on how Maryam changes during the extract.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight evidence and give answer frames. EAL: teach vocabulary of feelings. Stretch: infer how the sea is presented and why.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Reading skills for the SATs - The Lighthouse
lessons.title: Vocabulary in context and the effect of language
objectives: Explain the meaning of words and phrases in context
Explain how language choices affect the reader

keywords.def: surrounding words that help show meaning
a comparison using like or as
the feeling a word suggests
the impression made on the reader

starter: Bismillah. Make an inference: Her hands trembled.
Predict: The storm was getting worse.
Find and copy: the colour of the light on the water.

teach.heading: Meaning in context
bullets: Look at words around the word
Replace it with your own word
Check the sentence still makes sense
teach.note: Model: 'the sea heaved' - find a similar word: rose and fell with great force. Do not just give a dictionary definition if the question says 'in this context'.

teach.heading: Key words from the text
teach.note: Pupils choose the best meaning from options. Explain how to eliminate wrong choices. Use another word with the same meaning and test in the sentence.

teach.heading: Similes and effect
bullets: like a wild animal trapped in a cage
Explain: the sea wants to escape and is dangerous
teach.note: Break down the comparison: wild animal = fierce, unpredictable; cage = trapped, struggling. Teach the structure: technique, quotation, effect on the reader.

teach.heading: Word choice
bullets: heaved and roared: the sea sounds alive
teach.note: Ask pupils how the sea 'roared' is different from 'moved'. Discuss how verbs give the sea personality. Link to personification.

teach.heading: Write an effect answer
teach.note: Provide a model: 'The word "roared" makes the sea sound like an angry animal, which makes the reader feel the danger.' Pupils write their own.

practice: What does the word 'jagged' suggest about the rocks?
What impression does the phrase 'trapped in a cage' give of the sea?
Find and copy a word that shows how slowly the ship turned.
independent: Answer eight vocabulary and language questions.
Explain the effect of two phrases in full sentences.
Write a simile of your own to describe a storm.
exit: What does 'bobbed' suggest about the light?
Complete: The simile suggests the sea is...
lessons.homework: Choose two vivid phrases from a book and explain their effect.
lessons.send: SEND: vocabulary cards with images. EAL: pre-teach key verbs. Stretch: compare how the sea and Maryam are presented.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Reading skills for the SATs - The Lighthouse
lessons.title: Summarising, structure and comparison
objectives: Summarise a paragraph or section
Explain how the order of ideas affects meaning

keywords.def: give the main points briefly
how a text is organised
say how two things are similar or different
a group of sentences about one idea

starter: Bismillah. Explain the effect of the word 'roared'.
Find and copy: what Maryam used to signal.
Define 'jagged' in your own words.

teach.heading: Summarising
teach.note: Model summarising paragraph 3: Maryam keeps the lamp burning and spots a ship, which she signals. Explain that a summary is short. SAT questions often ask for a short summary of what a paragraph is about.

teach.heading: Match summaries
bullets: Choose the best title for each paragraph
Para 3: the signal; para 4: the ship turns
teach.note: Ask pupils to match headings to paragraphs. Include a wrong heading and discuss why it does not fit. Link to answering 'Which of these best summarises...?'

teach.heading: Structure
teach.note: Ask why the author describes the sea first. It sets the mood and danger. Explain how the order of ideas builds tension: setting, instruction, action, outcome.

teach.heading: Comparing
bullets: Compare Maryam at the start and end
End: smiled, let out a breath
teach.note: Teach comparative language. Write one sentence comparing the beginning and end. Ask for evidence. Also compare Maryam and her father.

teach.heading: Write a comparison answer
teach.note: Model: 'At the start, Maryam is anxious because she presses her nose against the glass; at the end, she smiles, which shows relief.' Pupils produce their own.

practice: Which is the best title for paragraph 2?
Why does the author begin with a description of the sea?
How is Maryam different at the end of the extract?
independent: Write a one-sentence summary of each paragraph.
Answer four structure and comparison questions.
Compare Maryam and her father in a short paragraph.
exit: Summarise paragraph 3 in one sentence.
Write one comparison word.
lessons.homework: Summarise a chapter of a book you are reading in three sentences.
lessons.send: SEND: matching headings to paragraphs. EAL: provide comparison sentence starters. Stretch: explain what would change if the story began with the signal.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Reading skills for the SATs - The Lighthouse
lessons.title: Timed reading practice and review
objectives: Apply reading skills to a new text under timed conditions
Review answers and set targets

keywords.def: planning how long to spend on each section
a skill to improve next
guidance showing what earns marks
look back and improve

starter: Bismillah. Name the eight reading skills (vocabulary, retrieval, ...).
What should you do first when reading a text?
How can you check an inference answer?

teach.heading: Plan your time
teach.note: Explain the pacing plan. In the real test pupils may use the whole hour; this plan helps. Model starting with easy questions.

teach.heading: Question types
teach.note: Show how each question type is answered. Provide a quick example for each from The Lighthouse. Remind them to read instructions carefully.

teach.heading: Mark scheme thinking
bullets: 2 marks need two points or point + evidence
Accept different wording if the meaning is right
teach.note: Share simplified mark scheme language. Explain that precise, relevant answers earn marks and that vague answers do not. Ask pupils to improve a weak answer.

teach.heading: Practise
teach.note: Share the unseen text (Layla's Market Stall, below) and set the questions in the independent task. Layla's Market Stall. Every Saturday, Layla helped her grandfather set up his stall in the old market square. By seven o'clock, the air smelled of cinnamon and fresh bread. Her grandfather arranged the dates in neat pyramids while Layla polished the brass scales until they gleamed. 'Customers buy with their eyes first,' he told her, smiling. By midday, a long queue snaked around the fountain. Layla weighed, wrapped and counted change as quickly as she could, though her arms ached. When the last customer had gone, her grandfather pressed a small bag of dates into her hands. 'For the best assistant in the market,' he said. Layla grinned: she had never felt so proud. Monitor timing. Encourage calm. Say a short dua before starting if desired.

teach.heading: Review and set targets
teach.note: Go through answers. Ask pupils to identify the kind of question they missed. Write a target such as 'use a quotation in inference answers'.

practice: Order these steps: answer, read, check.
How many marks would you give for two correct facts?
Which skill is 'give the meaning of a word in context'?
independent: Timed (15 minutes), on Layla's Market Stall: (1) What did the air smell of by seven o'clock? (2) Find and copy one word showing how shiny the scales were. (3) What does 'snaked' suggest about the queue? (4) Why did Layla's arms ache? (5) How did Layla feel at the end? Use evidence.
Mark your work using the mark scheme your teacher shares.
Write two targets for next time.
exit: Name your weakest reading skill.
Write your first target.
lessons.homework: Complete the next set of reading questions and bring your target to class.
lessons.send: SEND: reduce the number of questions and give extra time. EAL: use a bilingual dictionary for the pre-reading stage. Stretch: write your own question for each skill.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Writing formally and SATs review
lessons.title: Writing a formal persuasive letter
objectives: Plan and write a formal letter to persuade
Use the passive voice, subjunctive and formal vocabulary

keywords.def: convince someone to agree with you
a letter written in a polite, careful style
a question asked for effect, not for an answer
facts or reasons that support your argument

starter: Bismillah. Make formal: I want more books.
Complete with the subjunctive: If I (was/were) the headteacher...
Active or passive: A new library was built.

teach.heading: The task
bullets: Persuade them to create a quiet reading corner
teach.note: Set the scene: a school wants to improve reading. Pupils write a letter proposing a reading corner. Link to the value of seeking knowledge in Islam without making false claims: for example, the first revealed word of the Qur'an is 'Read' (Iqra), Surah al-Alaq 96:1.

teach.heading: Layout
teach.note: Show the layout. Explain that 'Yours sincerely' is used when you know the person's name. Point out punctuation and paragraphs. Model the first line.

teach.heading: Persuasive techniques
teach.note: Model sentences: 'Would you not agree that every pupil deserves a calm space to read?' 'A reading corner could transform our school.' Use modals to suggest rather than demand.

teach.heading: Formal grammar
bullets: Passive: A reading corner could be created.
Subjunctive: I suggest that the room be used.
teach.note: Point out that these features are what the SATs test and what formal writing needs. Model a paragraph combining all features.

teach.heading: Plan and write
teach.note: Pupils plan with four boxes and then draft. Circulate to check formal language. Encourage varied sentence structures.

practice: Write a formal opening sentence for your letter.
Write a sentence with a modal verb to suggest an idea.
Write a sentence using the subjunctive.
independent: Write the first two paragraphs of your letter.
Include a rhetorical question and one passive sentence.
Underline the formal vocabulary you used.
exit: Name one feature of formal writing used in your letter.
How will you end your letter?
lessons.homework: Finish your letter and check the formality.
lessons.send: SEND: use a letter template with prompts. EAL: provide formal phrases. Stretch: add a counter-argument and answer it.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Writing formally and SATs review
lessons.title: GPS and spelling review: mini-test and next steps
objectives: Complete a mini GPS test and spelling check
Identify and plan to improve weaker areas

keywords.def: look back at learning
something to work on next
a word that sounds the same as another but has a different spelling or meaning
a letter in a word that is not pronounced

starter: Bismillah. Spell: necessary, February, definitely.
Choose the right word: their / there / they're.
Name three punctuation marks learnt this half term.

teach.heading: Plan the lesson
teach.note: Explain how today works. Create a calm test atmosphere. Remind pupils that mistakes show us what to practise. Say bismillah and begin.

teach.heading: Spelling patterns
teach.note: Review common SATs spelling patterns. Pupils practise on whiteboards. Teach quick strategies: break words into syllables, use mnemonics, check root words.

teach.heading: Mini GPS test
teach.note: Provide the test. Read each question once. Time 15 minutes. Collect answers and then go through them together. Tell pupils to cross out and replace instead of rubbing out.

teach.heading: Mark and analyse
teach.note: Pupils tally errors by topic and identify their weakest area. Model this with a sample paper. Praise improvement.

teach.heading: Set targets
teach.note: Pupils write SMART targets. Share a few. Close by thanking Allah for the opportunity to learn and encouraging steady effort.

practice: Spell: necessary, February, definitely, queue, rhythm.
Choose: The (affect/effect) of the storm was huge.
Insert punctuation: The shop opened at nine it closed at five.
independent: Complete the mini GPS test (15 questions).
Take the 10-word spelling check.
Mark your paper and record your score.
exit: Which topic did you find hardest?
Write one target for the next half term.
lessons.homework: Practise your weakest topic with five new questions.
lessons.send: SEND: use a shorter test with larger print. EAL: allow bilingual dictionaries in the practice stage. Stretch: write your own GPS questions for a partner.
